newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan refining merger may fuel more alliances.
newsitem.headline: Japan refining merger may fuel more alliances.

text.p: A refining division merger of two of Japan"s leading oil firms could set off a wave of similar alliances as refiners face increasing pressure to survive, analysts and industry sources said on Monday.
Showa Shell Sekiyu KK said on Monday that it was considering merging its oil refining and distribution divisions with those of Mitsubishi Oil Co Ltd, but leaving the retail units separate.
It said a final agreement had yet to be reached.
"The potential alliance should accelerate cooperation and mergers between other oil firms," Toshinori Itoh, senior analyst with Daiwa Institute of Research, said.
"After hearing the news, other Japanese refiners are expected to consider countermeasures," he said.
A refining merger of Showa Shell Sekiyu, owned 50 percent by the Royal Dutch/Shell Group, and Mitsubishi Oil would spawn Japan"s largest refiner in capacity terms.
Analysts also said the decision by the two firms to keep their sales operations, and therefore their brand names, apart, would avoid market confusion and focus their sales activity.

"By keeping the sales divisions separate, Showa and Mitsubishi would need to pay more attention to making profits there," Hiroki Uchida, economist with LTCB Research Institute said. "This would enhance competitiveness."

Idemitsu Kosan Co Ltd currently holds top place in refining capacity with a 17.3 percent share, while Nippon Oil Co boasts top sales of oil products with 15.5 percent of total market share, according to the latest trade ministry statistics.
Showa Shell ranks fifth in both oil products sales and refining capacity with a 10.4 percent market share in sales, while its refining capacity of accounts for 11.1 percent of Japan"s total capacity.
Mitsubishi Oil comes in sixth place with an 8.1 percent market share in sales and nine percent of Japan"s refining capacity, the trade ministry statistics show.

The coziness between the two top firms Nippon Oil and Idemitsu, who already supply each other with oil products to cut distribution costs, may have spurred Showa and Mitsubishi to joining forces, analysts said.

Nippon and Idemitsu have denied persistent industry rumours the two would eventually merge, though sources said oil firms should find it easier to create alliances with a company with which they already have cooperative ties.

Some analysts said Esso Sekiyu, the Japanese unit of U.S. oil giant Exxon Corp, and General Sekiyu K.K., in which Exxon owns a 49-percent stake, may be another likely match, as more firms seek partners.
Oil companies have suffered shrinking profits from poor oil product retail prices coupled with rising costs due to high crude oil prices and a weaker yen against the dollar.

Japanese refiners lost their monopoly on imports of products such as gasoline and kerosene after last year"s industry deregulation, and have found themselves ill-prepared for the competition from abroad.
In the run-up to liberalisation, oil product retail prices dived in expectation of cheap imports, and have not recovered.
"Efforts to rationalise within the company have been overwhelmed by deteriorating oil product prices," Mitsuaki Nabetani, managing director of Showa Shell told reporters.

On Friday, Mitsubishi Oil estimated a parent current loss for the year of 9.5 billion yen ($76.6 million), revising down its earlier forecast of a profit of eight billion yen ($64.5 million). ($1=124 yen)
